title: Scientists say decades-old theory on the origin of life might be wrong
content: The popular theory that comets were crucial in kick-starting life on Earth billions of years ago may not hold up, according to new computer simulations that counter decades of scientific thinking. The finding suggests the fragile organic molecules supposedly carried by the icy objects would have been destroyed on impact, upending an established origin of life theory that dates back to at least 1961 . The broader idea that the ingredients for life arrived from space, known as panspermia , is even older and was scientifically postulated in 1908 . Life on Earth requires complex organic molecules, but it’s unclear whether our early planet had enough of the raw materials needed for prebiotic chemistry — the chemical reactions that produce the building blocks of life. Comets are made of dust and ice but are also known to contain organic material. This composition, which has earned the celestial bodies the nickname “dirty snowballs,” prompted scientists to suggest that comets could have deposited water and organic molecules on Earth’s surface. Early in its history — over 4 billion years ago — Earth may have experienced a period of heavy bombardment from more than 100,000 comets larger than 100 meters (328 feet), according to the new study, published Wednesday in the journal Scientific Reports . Those impacts, however, were mostly too heavy for life-starting molecules to withstand. The team used the latest models of comet formation and evolution to simulate this early planetary period 100,000 times. “Given what we know about surface environments on the early Earth, on average, our simulations found that there were no successful impacts,” said lead study author Richard Anslow, who conducted the research while completing his doctorate at the Institute of Astronomy of the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom. The comets contained large concentrations of key molecules needed for life, but the simulation found the objects were coming in too fast to successfully deposit them. “The typical velocities of these comets when they impact the Earth meant that actually very few, if any, would have been able to deliver intact organic molecules, so comets actually don’t seem to be as useful for prebiotic chemistry as was previously thought,” Anslow said. More precisely, 54% of the simulations showed no impact at all, while the remaining 46% had at least one and a “tiny minority” returned up to three collisions, Anslow said. “We can’t rule out confidently that there was never a successful impact — there could have been one of these fluke impacts.” However, such flukes had to occur in a “perfect location” that already met several important conditions, including the presence of liquid water and other chemicals needed to support life. That combination makes the overall process unlikely, he added. The study focuses on a naturally occurring chemical called hydrogen cyanide or HCN, an important precursor in prebiotic chemistry that has been detected in dozens of comets, including the notable Halley’s and Hale-Bopp comets. Composed of hydrogen, carbon and nitrogen, HCN can lead to the formation of amino acids — molecules that make up proteins — when combined with water; other studies have previously identified HCN as a potential key ingredient for the origin of life on Earth. “When comets strike Earth, they’re shocked to high temperatures and pressures, and recent studies have found that a lot of these precursor molecules can be destroyed by this high pressure and temperature as well as the following impacts,” Anslow said. The study authors argue that even if a successful impact occurred, it’s unlikely that it would have delivered the chemical in a useful concentration, and in the case of an ocean impact, it would have quickly dissolved. To set the stage for prebiotic chemistry to occur, many other precursor molecules are also needed, such as compounds that contain phosphorus and sulfur, but these are not routinely found in comets, Anslow said. “Comets are really good for delivering hydrogen cyanide, but given it’s random where a comet impacts onto Earth, we’re not going to be guaranteed to have everything else that we need for this chemistry right in that spot.” If comets didn’t deliver the building blocks of life on Earth, Anslow said there are several other promising avenues to explore. Another long-held , competing theory is the possibility that Earth’s primordial soup could have synthesized the molecules needed for life on its own. An alternative cosmic source of organic material could have been asteroids, which typically struck Earth more slowly and in greater numbers. Anslow pointed to recent findings on samples from asteroids Bennu and Ryugu, which contain the majority of protein-building amino acids. The recent study also raises another intriguing possibility: While Earth may not have had the ideal conditions to foster HCN from comet impacts, ancient Mars might have been better suited . “Because Mars is much smaller than Earth and further away from the sun, the typical impact velocity of comets is much lower, so while these impacts on Earth were destroying most of the HCN, this wasn’t the case so much for Mars,” Anslow said. This idea could add another dimension to the long-standing question of whether the red planet once supported life. “It’s just another perspective to have in the back of our minds when we’re trying to understand the early evolution of Mars in more detail,” Anslow said. While the authors closely analyzed how HCN could have survived comet impact, the chemical may have undergone reactions before the icy bodies entered Earth’s atmosphere, said Queenie Chan, an associate professor of Earth sciences at Royal Holloway University of London, who was not involved with the study. This process could have created biologically important compounds, such as those protein building blocks, that are less volatile and more likely to survive. “Therefore, the inefficiency of delivering intact HCN does not completely rule out a potential role for comets in supplying other important organic compounds that may have contributed to Earth’s prebiotic organic inventory before the emergence of life,” Chan wrote in an email. Nicolle Zellner, a professor of physics at Albion College in Michigan, said in an email that she wasn’t surprised by the findings. While she is also reluctant to eliminate comets as a possible contributor to the emergence of life, she acknowledged that “the authors have definitely put some good parameters around the likelihood.”

content: Proteins commonly associated with Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease may have a surprising function in human reproduction. Researchers at Columbia University’s Zuckerman Institute have discovered that amyloid fibrils, tiny protein fibers found in semen, can help transport RNA into sperm cells. The findings suggest a previously unknown pathway for moving genetic material into sperm and could eventually lead to new methods for delivering gene therapies. Published in Molecular Cell , the research shows that amyloids can serve a useful biological purpose despite their association with neurodegenerative diseases. The scientists also demonstrated that these protein fibers can carry RNA molecules large enough to produce functional proteins in developing embryos. The investigation grew out of earlier research showing that amyloid fibrils in semen can help HIV enter cells in the reproductive tract. Anthony Fitzpatrick, PhD, a Columbia researcher who studies amyloids in brain diseases, wondered whether these same structures might help transport the body’s own genetic material into sperm. His team focused on RNA, a molecule involved in converting genetic instructions into proteins and regulating gene activity. Seminal fluid contains numerous small RNA molecules that may influence gene expression during embryonic development. However, scientists have not fully understood how these molecules move from semen into sperm. HIV provided a potential connection because the virus uses RNA as its genetic material. If seminal amyloids could facilitate viral entry into cells, researchers reasoned, they might also help deliver free RNA molecules. William Mallen, PhD, the study’s lead author, investigated whether amyloid fibrils could attach to RNA. The two have complementary electrical properties: amyloids carry a positive charge, while RNA is negatively charged. Using fluorescent markers, Mallen confirmed that the molecules bind together. The researchers proposed that amyloids might also protect RNA during transport. RNA is relatively fragile and can be broken down by enzymes, whereas amyloid fibrils form highly stable structures. Encasing RNA within these fibers could potentially help preserve it, although that protective function has not yet been established. To determine whether the fibrils actually enter sperm, the team used cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), a powerful imaging technique that creates detailed three-dimensional views of frozen biological samples. Amyloid fibers marked with tiny gold particles were found inside sperm cells, confirming that they could cross the cell boundary rather than simply attach to its surface. “Seeing those amyloid fibers inside sperm cells was just so extraordinary to me,” said Mallen, who is now a medical student at the University of Vermont. “There were hints of this happening earlier in our other experiments, but actually seeing this just totally blew us away.” Additional experiments using fluorescent markers showed that amyloid fibrils greatly increased the amount of RNA entering sperm. The researchers also identified a possible mechanism for releasing the transported material: a protein called clusterin could help separate RNA from its amyloid carrier once inside cells. The team tested whether the fibrils could deliver larger RNA molecules capable of directing protein production. Sperm exposed to amyloid-bound RNA encoding green fluorescent protein were used in fertilization experiments. The resulting embryos produced at least 10 times more of the fluorescent protein than embryos fertilized with sperm exposed to the same RNA without amyloids. Previous studies have suggested that RNA carried by sperm can influence gene activity in offspring through epigenetic mechanisms, which regulate how genes are used without altering the underlying DNA sequence. Research in mice has also linked paternal transmission of certain metabolic conditions, including insulin resistance, to RNA-mediated processes. Beyond reproduction, the findings could have implications for RNA delivery in medicine. Technologies such as CRISPR rely on RNA to guide gene-editing machinery toward specific DNA sequences, but getting these components safely and efficiently into cells remains a major challenge. Some gene therapies use modified viruses to transport genetic material into cells. Although effective in many applications, viral delivery systems can provoke immune responses. Amyloid fibrils derived from human proteins might eventually provide another approach, although their safety and effectiveness as therapeutic carriers still require investigation. “Since the amyloid fibrils we looked at are human-based, hopefully the immune system won’t react in the same way they do to the repurposed viruses often used in gene therapy,” Mallen said. Reference: “Amyloid-mediated RNA uptake by sperm for embryonic delivery” by William S. Mallen, Nataliya Zabello, Susan Brenner-Morton, Simone Sidoli, Feng-Xia Liang, Joseph Sall, Jason Yin, Priyanka Mathews, Mengmeng Zhu, Guoan Zhang, Carolyn L. Lee, Ya-Cheng Liao and Anthony W.P. Fitzpatrick, 26 October 2026, Molecular Cell . content: Uranus and Neptune have long been considered planetary twins, but new research suggests their similarities may conceal surprisingly different origins. Neptune may have formed from material that originated much closer to the young Sun, challenging the long-standing belief that it and Uranus developed from the same reservoir of cosmic ingredients. New research suggests the two ice giants, despite their striking similarities, have significantly different chemical histories. An international research team, including scientists from Southwest Research Institute (SwRI), found evidence that Neptune’s deep atmosphere contains substantially more oxygen than Uranus’s. Published in the September 2026 issue of Astronomy & Astrophysics , the study uses atmospheric observations and computer models to investigate how the planets acquired their chemical compositions roughly 4.5 billion years ago. Uranus and Neptune have comparable sizes, masses, and atmospheric conditions, making them appear almost like planetary twins. Neither has a solid surface like Earth. Instead, their atmospheres extend thousands of miles into their interiors, with water, ammonia, and methane among the compounds present. Methane in their upper atmospheres helps produce their distinctive blue-green colors by absorbing red wavelengths of sunlight. “Uranus and Neptune may resemble twins today, but their chemistry is telling us that they are more like cousins with very different histories,” said Dr. Olivier Mousis, a program director in SwRI’s Solar System Science and Exploration Division in Boulder, Colorado, and a co-author of the study. “Their atmospheric compositions may be connected to different regions of the protoplanetary disk where the planets formed, which would make their similarities a noteworthy coincidence.” To investigate the planets’ chemical differences, researchers analyzed carbon monoxide measurements, including recent observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA). Although scientists cannot directly sample the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, carbon monoxide concentrations in their upper atmospheres can help constrain the chemistry of the layers below. The team combined these observations with atmospheric chemistry models to estimate oxygen abundances and carbon-to-oxygen ratios. Their results indicate that Neptune’s deeper atmosphere is considerably more oxygen-rich than Uranus’s, suggesting that the two planets incorporated different proportions of carbon-bearing and oxygen-bearing materials during formation. “We can’t directly access the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, but chemical tracers allow us to probe the conditions hidden beneath their visible clouds,” Mousis said. “Studying carbon monoxide, or CO, is particularly useful because of its abundance in the upper troposphere. Using this data, we can model the chemical evolution of the protoplanetary disk and the origins of its materials.” The researchers then examined how these chemical differences could have developed within the protoplanetary disk, the rotating collection of gas and dust surrounding the young Sun. As the disk cooled, volatile compounds condensed into solids at different temperatures and distances. This process created reservoirs of material with distinct chemical compositions, providing different ingredients for growing planets. By comparing the planets’ inferred carbon-to-oxygen ratios with models of the evolving disk, the team identified a possible explanation for Neptune’s unusual composition. Rather than forming entirely from materials available near its present orbit, Neptune may have accumulated building blocks that originated closer to the Sun and subsequently migrated outward. This would give Neptune a different chemical history from Uranus, even if the two planets formed during roughly the same period. “Neptune’s chemistry is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it formed where we see it today, pulling from the same reservoir of cosmic materials as Uranus,” Mousis said. “Instead, our models lead us to believe that its building blocks traveled a long way to where Neptune could accrete them. In short, two superficially similar worlds may have reached their present locations and formations through two very distinct evolutionary paths.” The proposed formation scenario remains dependent on atmospheric and planetary formation models. Without direct measurements from deep within Uranus and Neptune, scientists cannot fully determine their internal compositions or reconstruct the movement of materials that shaped them. Future spacecraft observations and atmospheric probes could provide more precise constraints on their chemistry and formation histories. “Our findings have implications beyond Neptune and Uranus and even far beyond our Solar System,” Mousis said. “Planets comparable in size to Uranus and Neptune are common around other stars, which is why Uranus and Neptune are essential benchmarks for understanding how planets form and evolve throughout the galaxy, and it is precisely why missions like NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe, expected to launch sometime in the next decade, are so important.” Reference: “Contrasting C/O ratios in Uranus and Neptune from disequilibrium chemistry: A clue to distinct evolutionary pathways?” by T. Briand, V. Hue, O. Mousis, T. Cavalié, T. Benest Couzinou, A. Schneeberger and M. D. Hofstadter, 19 October 2026, Astronomy & Astrophysics .
